title: Ellen Halliday
gist: An author index page (not an article) for Ellen Halliday, deputy editor of Prospect; her 13 listed pieces show a climate-politics beat built on interviews with Sir David King, Eliane Brum, Sophia Kianni and Conor Gearty, plus framing questions on heatwave scepticism, a possible deep freeze, green growth and lawyers switching sides from polluters to the planet.

insights.claim: Prospect's deputy editor frames heatwave scepticism as evidence of a broader climate delusion, treating public denial of visible extreme heat as the phenomenon to explain rather than the science.
insights.speaker: Prospect Magazine
insights.so_what: Persistent public denial of observable physical climate risk slows adaptation spending even as insured losses rise.
insights.quote: Heatwave sceptics reveal our climate delusion
insights.locator: Climate Change / Heatwave sceptics reveal our climate delusion

insights.claim: Alongside heat coverage, the same editor asks whether a deep freeze is coming, indicating mainstream UK ideas journalism is treating abrupt cold-side climate disruption as a serious scenario rather than only warming.
insights.speaker: Prospect Magazine
insights.so_what: Two-tailed climate scenarios (heat plus abrupt cooling) widen the range of energy-demand and infrastructure stress cases to plan for.
insights.locator: Climate / Is a deep freeze coming?

themes.theme: Climate elites, activists and legal pressure

insights.claim: Climate expert Sir David King is quoted saying the UK has made itself look very small on the international scene, a former chief scientific adviser's judgement on lost British climate leadership.
insights.speaker: Prospect Magazine
insights.so_what: Loss of UK diplomatic standing on climate weakens its ability to set standards that UK-listed climate-exposed firms benefit from.
insights.quote: We have made ourselves look very small on the international scene
insights.locator: People / Climate expert Sir David King

insights.claim: The beat features a barrister pushing lawyers to back the planet rather than polluters, plus activist Sophia Kianni arguing countries must put their money where their mouth is, signalling litigation and finance-accountability as the active pressure channels.
insights.speaker: Prospect Magazine
insights.so_what: Professional-services defection from fossil clients raises legal costs and reputational risk for high-emitting firms.
insights.quote: The barrister pushing lawyers to back the planet, not polluters

insights.claim: Brazilian journalist Eliane Brum is quoted arguing hope will not save us from climate change and that the fight is for life itself, marking a shift in activist framing from optimism to survival.
insights.speaker: Prospect Magazine
insights.so_what: Radicalising activist rhetoric raises the probability of disruptive protest and confrontational campaigning against carbon-intensive projects.
insights.quote: hope won’t save us from climate change. We should be fighting for life

insights.claim: The green-growth question is posed as still open rather than settled in Prospect's climate coverage, alongside a profile of the forecaster who stops the Thames from flooding — pairing macro decarbonisation debate with concrete adaptation infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Prospect Magazine
insights.so_what: Adaptation infrastructure (flood defence, forecasting) gets attention as the decoupling debate stalls — a spending category likely to grow either way.
insights.locator: Climate Change / Is green growth the future?

insights.claim: The same editor covers civil liberties through Conor Gearty's call to have some fights with the right enemies and attacks the hypocrisy of hard-right self-styled protectors, linking climate politics to a broader rights-and-authoritarianism frame.
insights.speaker: Prospect Magazine
insights.so_what: Climate and civil-liberties agendas are converging in UK liberal media, foreshadowing conflict over protest policing and rights legislation.
insights.quote: Let’s have some fights with the right enemies
